claims.text: In situ high-resolution TEM during synthesis will enable controlled formation of noble metal-based HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Synchrotron-based X-ray absorption spectroscopy during synthesis will enable controlled formation of noble metal-based HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
In situ characterization-assisted synthesis will produce a more homogeneous atomic distribution than conventional synthesis.
Conventional synthesis of noble metal-based HEAs typically produces heterogeneous atomic distributions.
In situ electron microscopy can monitor atomic-scale structural and chemical evolution of a noble-metal-containing HEA under heating.
In situ high-resolution TEM or XAS can be used to adjust alloy formation in real time.
The proposed method can operate in controlled high-temperature environments.
The proposed method is applicable under high-temperature reduction or controlled-atmosphere synthesis conditions used for catalytic material preparation.
Direct real-time characterization feedback can guide atomic-scale formation of a nanoframework.
In situ electron imaging can detect atomic-scale structural and chemical events during heating of HEA nanoparticles.
In situ spectral analysis can immediately detect transient atomic-scale events during HEA formation.
Real-time characterization feedback enables synthesis-parameter adjustments that promote uniform and controlled HEA self-assembly.
The intervention will produce three-dimensional HEA nanoframeworks with enhanced atomic uniformity.
The resulting nanoframeworks will have predictable surface configurations.
Enhanced atomic uniformity and predictable surface configurations are expected to improve catalytic performance.
Conventional synthesis yields HEA structures with heterogeneous alloying and less-controlled surface architectures.
The method is likely limited to laboratory-scale synthesis under precisely controlled conditions.
Industrial-scale production would require further adaptation of the method.
The degree of atomic-control improvement depends on synthesis parameters and measurement sensitivity.
